subject: math
cluster: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems
intro: Units are a tool for thinking, not just labels you attach at the end. A conversion factor is a fraction equal to $1$, like $\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}$, that you orient so the unit you want to remove cancels. By carrying units through every multiplication and division, you can check that a setup is correct: a good setup is one whose units cancel to leave exactly the units the question asks for. The same habit lets you keep units consistent before substituting into a formula, figure out the units of an unknown, and choose a sensible scale and origin when you graph data.

items.prompt: Convert $7$ feet to inches using the fact that $1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}$.

steps: Write the conversion factor as a fraction equal to $1$. Since we want to cancel feet, put feet in the denominator: $\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}$.
Multiply the given quantity by the conversion factor: $7\text{ ft}\times\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}$.
The ft unit cancels, leaving inches: $7\times 12\text{ in}=84\text{ in}$.
Check: the only unit left is inches, which is what the question asked for.

items.prompt: Convert $2.5$ miles to inches using $1\text{ mi}=5280\text{ ft}$ and $1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}$.

steps: Chain two conversion factors so the intermediate unit (feet) cancels. Orient each so the unwanted unit is on the bottom.
Set up: $2.5\text{ mi}\times\frac{5280\text{ ft}}{1\text{ mi}}\times\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}$.
The mi cancels with mi and the ft cancels with ft, leaving inches.
Multiply the numbers: $2.5\times 5280=13200$, then $13200\times 12=158400$.
Check: only inches remain, so the setup is correct.

items.prompt: A car travels at $60\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$. Convert this speed to $\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$ using $1\text{ mi}=5280\text{ ft}$ and $1\text{ hr}=3600\text{ s}$.

steps: This is a compound rate, so convert the numerator (miles to feet) and the denominator (hours to seconds).
Convert miles to feet with $\frac{5280\text{ ft}}{1\text{ mi}}$ so the mi cancels.
Convert hours to seconds with $\frac{1\text{ hr}}{3600\text{ s}}$ so the hr cancels (hr is in the denominator of the rate, so we need hr in the numerator of the factor).
Set up: $60\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}\times\frac{5280\text{ ft}}{1\text{ mi}}\times\frac{1\text{ hr}}{3600\text{ s}}$.
After cancelling mi and hr, the units left are $\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$.
Check: the units are $\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$, exactly what was requested.

items.prompt: Using $\text{distance}=\text{rate}\times\text{time}$, a runner moves at $8\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$ for $5$ minutes. How far does the runner travel, in feet?

steps: Make the units consistent before substituting. The rate uses seconds but the time is in minutes, so convert.
Convert $5$ minutes to seconds: $5\text{ min}\times\frac{60\text{ s}}{1\text{ min}}=300\text{ s}$.
Substitute into $d=\text{rate}\times\text{time}$: $d=8\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}\times 300\text{ s}$.
The s cancels, leaving feet: $d=8\times 300\text{ ft}=2400\text{ ft}$.
Check: the answer is in feet, the unit the formula produces once the inputs match.

items.prompt: In the work formula $W=Fd$, force $F$ is measured in newtons (N) and distance $d$ in meters (m). What are the units of $W$? Also explain how unit reasoning rules out reporting $W$ in newtons alone.

steps: Units multiply the same way the quantities do. Since $W=Fd$, the units of $W$ are (units of $F$)$\times$(units of $d$).
That gives $\text{N}\times\text{m}=\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$.
A newton-meter is also called a joule (J), so $W$ is in joules.
Reporting $W$ in N alone would drop the meter factor entirely, which cannot be right because $d$ contributes its meters to the product. The units must include both N and m.

items.prompt: Convert $48$ inches to feet using $1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}$.
items.hint: Orient the conversion factor so the inches cancel. That means inches should be in the denominator: $\frac{1\text{ ft}}{12\text{ in}}$.

steps: Write the factor so inches cancel: $\frac{1\text{ ft}}{12\text{ in}}$.
Multiply: $48\text{ in}\times\frac{1\text{ ft}}{12\text{ in}}$.
The in cancels, leaving feet: $\frac{48}{12}\text{ ft}=4\text{ ft}$.

items.prompt: Convert $3$ kilometers to centimeters using $1\text{ km}=1000\text{ m}$ and $1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}$.
items.hint: Chain two factors so that km cancels first, then m cancels, leaving cm.

steps: Set up the chain: $3\text{ km}\times\frac{1000\text{ m}}{1\text{ km}}\times\frac{100\text{ cm}}{1\text{ m}}$.
The km cancels with km and the m cancels with m, leaving centimeters.
Multiply: $3\times 1000=3000$, then $3000\times 100=300000$.

items.prompt: A hose fills a tank at $3\ \frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}$. How many gallons does the tank hold if it fills completely in $2$ hours? Use $1\text{ hr}=60\text{ min}$.
items.hint: Convert the time to minutes first so it matches the rate, then multiply rate by time.

steps: Convert $2$ hours to minutes: $2\text{ hr}\times\frac{60\text{ min}}{1\text{ hr}}=120\text{ min}$.
Multiply rate by time: $3\ \frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\times 120\text{ min}$.
The min cancels, leaving gallons: $3\times 120\text{ gal}=360\text{ gal}$.

items.prompt: A cyclist rides at $30\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$. Convert this speed to $\frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$ using $1\text{ mi}=5280\text{ ft}$ and $1\text{ hr}=3600\text{ s}$.
items.hint: Both the numerator and the denominator change. Use $\frac{1\text{ mi}}{5280\text{ ft}}$ to cancel feet and $\frac{3600\text{ s}}{1\text{ hr}}$ to cancel seconds.

steps: Set up: $30\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}\times\frac{1\text{ mi}}{5280\text{ ft}}\times\frac{3600\text{ s}}{1\text{ hr}}$.
The ft cancels and the s cancels, leaving $\frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$.
So the speed is about $20.45\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$.

items.prompt: Daily high temperatures for a week range from $52^{\circ}\text{F}$ to $89^{\circ}\text{F}$. You will plot them on a vertical axis. Choose a reasonable starting value (origin) and a scale (interval per gridline) for the axis, and justify why starting at $0$ would be a poor choice.
items.hint: The data is clustered far from zero. Pick an origin a little below the smallest value and a scale that spreads the range of about $37^{\circ}\text{F}$ across several gridlines.

steps: Find the range of the data: $89^{\circ}\text{F}-52^{\circ}\text{F}=37^{\circ}\text{F}$.
Choose an origin just below the lowest value so the data is not squeezed against the bottom. Starting at $50^{\circ}\text{F}$ works well.

Choose a scale that covers the range in a handful of gridlines. With a scale of $5^{\circ}\text{F}$ per gridline, the axis from $50^{\circ}\text{F}$ to $90^{\circ}\text{F}$ uses $8$ gridlines, which displays the data clearly.
Starting at $0^{\circ}\text{F}$ would waste the entire $0$ to $50$ portion of the axis, compressing all the data into a small band at the top and hiding the day-to-day differences.
solution.answer: Start the axis near $50^{\circ}\text{F}$ (not $0$) and use a scale of about $5^{\circ}\text{F}$ per gridline; a $0$ origin wastes most of the axis and hides the variation.
